intro: How redundancy works in New Zealand, from when a role can be cut to notice, final pay and compensation, and the different rules for high income earners.
explanation:
## What redundancy is

A person is made redundant when their job ends because the role is no longer needed, which employers call disestablishing it. It comes out of a workplace change or restructure, and a set redundancy process has to be followed. Moving the employee into another suitable role, called redeployment or technical redundancy, needs the same process. So does voluntary redundancy, where the employer invites staff to leave. A sale or transfer of the business has separate rules, and so does an employer's liquidation or bankruptcy.

## When a role can be cut

Two things must be true: there is a genuine business reason, such as improved technology or financial pressures, and the employer has weighed other options. Those options include changing hours, duties or shifts, saving money elsewhere, or moving people into other suitable roles. The employer keeps considering them through the whole process.

Some reasons are not allowed. A role cannot be cut because of personal reasons, discrimination, concerns about performance or concerns about behaviour, as performance and discipline have their own processes. If the employer hires someone for an identical or sufficiently similar role soon afterwards, that can suggest the role was still needed and the redundancy was not genuine.

## The process

Before any redundancy, even a voluntary one, the employer has to run a fair workplace change process. It runs from a written proposal with reasons, through identifying who may be affected, consultation with employees and unions and consideration of their feedback, to a decision and putting it into effect. Employment agreements and workplace policies may add steps.

A person on parental leave or ACC can still be made redundant, but being away cannot be the reason, and the employer should take extra care to involve them. Where the person is on parental leave or certain defence force leave, the employer has more to prove. The employer must be able to show four things: the leave is not behind the decision; the job was confirmed in writing as being held open before the redundancy arose; no substantially similar job is available; and leave time counts as service where service matters in the decision.

## Notice

Notice is owed as the employment agreement sets it, or, where the agreement says nothing, for a reasonable time. What counts as reasonable depends on matters such as the reason for the redundancy. The two sides can agree to shorten or lengthen it. If the employer wants a shorter period and the employee refuses, the employer pays for the full agreed notice.

An employee can ask to use leave they have not taken during the notice period, and the employer can decline annual holidays for a good reason. Paying out the notice period instead of working it, or sending the employee on garden leave, needs an agreement, whether a clause in the contract or one made when notice is given. Garden leave must be put in writing.

## Compensation and final pay

Redundancy compensation is not automatic. An employee can get it only if their employment agreement or a workplace policy provides for it, or they and the employer agree on it. If the employer offers another role, compensation is owed only where the employment agreement says so. An employee who turns down a suitable role without a good reason may get none. The agreement should set the amount, and if it does not, the two sides must agree one.

Final pay covers wages, holiday pay, any compensation and other amounts owed. On the last day the employee can request proof of their service, but no reference has to be supplied.

## Higher earners

Under the rules that began in February 2026, an employee who earns {fact:nz_red_hi} or more a year has fewer dismissal protections. The employer need not follow a fair process or have a good reason, including a genuine business reason for redundancy, and the employee generally cannot raise a personal grievance over the dismissal. Both sides can opt back in, in writing, and it covers every protection or none. The employer must still give the notice in the agreement, or a reasonable period, and meet the first two good faith principles.

During a transition period, an employee in the same job as before the change, or in a different job because of a restructure, can still raise a personal grievance if dismissed before {fact:nz_red_trans}. The grievance must be raised within {fact:nz_red_pg}. The threshold is reviewed each July.

## Challenging a redundancy

If the reason looks not genuine or the process was skipped, the employee's options are a personal grievance for unjustified dismissal or mediation.
